# Kestrel Smithing Handbook

Kestrel smiths work sky-iron, a metal that falls with the autumn storms. It must be heated slowly; quenching it in snow-melt gives the blade its blue sheen.

A good sword takes nine days. The first three are for folding, the next three for shaping, and the last three for tempering and the hilt.

## Tea and rest

Every smith keeps a kettle on the forge. Pine-needle tea is traditional: bitter, hot, and said to steady the hand. Apprentices brew it for the master at dawn and dusk.

## Names and debts

Debts are recorded in the guild ledger by name. Robert, the miller's son, currently owes three silver coins. Debts older than a season are read aloud at the autumn fair, which most people consider worse than paying.

## Feelings at the forge

Smiths say the fire listens. If you feel angry, the metal cracks; if you feel calm, it sings. Many smiths hum while they work for this reason.
